overview: This entry follows the map’s 1878 to 1914 coastal Gabon record during French colonial expansion. It is not the independent republic, and the communities living here did not begin when colonial administrators arrived. Gabon became part of French Equatorial Africa in 1910. Local family traditions, craft knowledge and river networks continued within a changing and unequal political setting.

periods.title: The map’s earlier colonial window
periods.summary: These opening dates belong to the imported map; they do not identify the founding of Gabonese communities.

periods.title: Within French Equatorial Africa
periods.summary: Gabon joined a federation with Middle Congo, Ubangi-Shari and Chad. The map stops this record four years later.

items.text: Fang families preserved important ancestors’ remains in bark containers protected by carved guardians. A nineteenth-century Okak-Fang figure at the Metropolitan Museum comes from Gabon or Equatorial Guinea. Its uncertain national attribution matters: the family networks behind these objects crossed the borders drawn on modern maps.

The guardian combines wood, copper alloy and palm oil. Its controlled posture and energetic forms express qualities admired by its makers. Museum displays usually separate such carvings from their original containers, so the sculpture alone reveals only part of an ensemble concerned with kinship, memory and protection.

A nineteenth-century Tsogo harp from Gabon has a wooden body, a skin belly and palm-fibre strings. Small studs beneath the skin hold the strings taut. Instrument making brought woodworking, skin preparation and careful adjustment together: a beautiful shape still had to produce a useful sound.

The harp was played upright, with its carved face near the musician’s own face. The museum connects instruments of this kind with women’s healing ceremonies. This records a relationship between music, care and spiritual life; it does not establish the medical effectiveness of a particular ritual.

sections.title: Food and travel beside the Ogooué

items.text: Writing in 1897, traveller Mary Kingsley described manioc being beaten in wooden troughs resembling miniature canoes. She said collectors sometimes mistook the pounding tools for weapons. Her account contains colonial prejudice, but this particular observation offers a memorable reminder that a dramatic-looking wooden object might belong in the kitchen.

Kingsley also described dough wrapped in plantain leaves and steamed in a covered pot. The leaves helped package the food while cooks managed the fire. These are observations from her travels, not a complete menu for every community or instructions for preparing raw cassava safely.

On the Ogooué, canoe crews used long poles as well as paddles to negotiate the water. Kingsley recorded obtaining replacement poles and another experienced helper before tackling rapids. River travel depended on local skill, not simply on drawing a confident line across a map.

At Kangwe mission, Kingsley stayed in a room normally used by schoolgirls. That small accommodation detail documents girls living and learning at this particular mission. It cannot tell us how many children across Gabon attended school, or replace the learning that happened within homes and communities.

Hélène and Albert Schweitzer arrived at Lambaréné in April 1913 and helped establish a hospital. Hélène served as the responsible nurse during their first stay. Remembering her work makes the hospital’s beginning a story about nursing and collaboration, alongside its better-known doctor.

Before travelling, Hélène undertook nursing training and gathered information about missions in the Congo region. Her preparation combined practical care and research. This is one documented medical institution within colonial Gabon, not evidence that local people had previously lacked ways of caring for illness.

sections.title: A written glimpse from the coast

items.text: A postcard of Port-Gentil, catalogued around 1910, carries the French words “Dans les Palétuviers”, meaning “In the mangroves”. The Smithsonian transcribes and translates the caption. This is an attested colonial printed sample, not a phrase in a local Gabonese language.

The postcard is a small monochrome print. Its caption directs the viewer toward a coastal landscape, while leaving the people’s own words unheard. Such objects document what publishers offered distant readers; a postcard is a selected view, not a whole community squeezed onto paper.

ending.text: The map’s 1914 endpoint is not Gabon’s independence or the disappearance of its peoples. French colonial rule continued beyond this record; the independent republic dates from 17 August 1960. The older coastal entry and the later Gabon card therefore describe different political periods.
